title: Azoth calculation spec
description: A single calculation in the Azoth registry. Every calc must declare its equation, a source, the range in which it is validated, its assumptions, a worked example, and the tests that exercise it. Docs and tests are generated from these files, so this schema is the single source of truth.

id.description: Dotted identifier, e.g. hydraulics.darcy_weisbach. Must match the module and function names in both implementations.

name.description: Human-readable name, used as the doc page title.

equation.description: The equation. Written in Python expression syntax where the equation is explicit, so the worked example can be independently re-derived from it. For implicit equations (e.g. Colebrook) it is the defining relation and the worked example is derived by the solver named in `solver`. Rendered as LaTeX in the generated docs.

latex.description: The equation in LaTeX, for the generated documentation. A separate field from `equation` because the two have different jobs: `equation` is Python source, machine-evaluable and used to re-derive the worked example, while `latex` is typeset for a reader. `equation` cannot be rendered as mathematics - `log10(rr / 3.7 + ...)` is not notation a human reads - and `latex` cannot be evaluated. spec_lint requires this field rather than making it optional, because a calc whose documentation shows no equation is the drift this project exists to prevent.

source.description: Where the equation comes from. The `equation` field here is the source's own equation number and may be 'TODO: source needed' when it cannot be verified.

standard.description: Name of the standard, textbook, or paper.

equation.description: Equation number within the source. Use 'TODO: source needed' if unverified.

verification.description: Whether a human has verified this spec against its primary source. Drives whether tests may run (enforced by tools/spec_lint.py).

status.description: verified = checked against the primary source. unverified = equation is standard but the citation is not confirmed. source_needed = no adequate source found; the worked_example test must be skipped.

inputs.description: Input quantities, keyed by parameter name. Key names must match the function signatures in both implementations exactly.

outputs.description: Output quantities, keyed by result field name. Key names must match the result struct fields in both implementations exactly.

valid_range.description: Bounds on the range in which the calc is validated. Typed bounds rather than free-form expressions, so they are machine-checkable and need no expression parser.

assumptions.description: Physical assumptions the calc relies on that are NOT checked at runtime. Documented, not enforced - keep checked constraints in valid_range.

references.description: Citations. Cite equations and papers; never reproduce copyrighted tables or text.

solver.description: Required for implicit equations. Encoding the solver in the spec is what keeps the Python and Rust implementations numerically comparable: a different-but-valid solver, or the same solver with a different stopping rule, would diverge in the last bits and fail the agreement test. Both implementations must implement exactly this scheme - see docs/src/theory/solvers.md.

kind.description: The scheme to solve with. Only `fixed_point` is implemented, in both languages, so it is the only value this enum permits: a spec naming `bisection` or `newton` would describe a calculation neither implementation can run, which is the 'looks like validation, does nothing' failure this schema exists to catch. Adding a kind means three things in one commit - the solver in both implementations, the cross-language agreement test that proves they run the same scheme, and a new contract test holding this enum and the implementations' solver kinds to each other the way test_warning_codes_match_the_schema holds the warning codes to the schema. Nothing does that for solver kinds today, which is why this enum is narrow rather than merely unchecked.

convergence.description: Stopping rule applied to successive iterates x_k. `relative` means |x_{k+1} - x_k| <= tolerance * |x_{k+1}|; `absolute` means |x_{k+1} - x_k| <= tolerance. Naming this explicitly matters: the same tolerance means different things under the two rules, and the two implementations must agree on which one is meant.

data.description: Repo-relative paths to data files this calc reads. One key per dataset.

worked_example.description: A fully specified example whose expected outputs are independently reproducible from the equation. This is the primary validation artefact.

source.description: Where the example comes from. Use 'derived from the equation above' when we computed it ourselves, and say so in `derivation`.

derivation.description: How the expected values were obtained. Required when source is our own derivation, so a reviewer can retrace it.

inputs.description: Input values in the units declared in `inputs`. Keys must be exactly the calc's input names, so the generated test can call the implementation directly.

expected.description: Expected output values in the units declared in `outputs`.

tests.description: Tests to generate and run. Every calc needs at least a worked_example; reference and property tests are strongly encouraged.

notes.description: Free-form reviewer notes. Not rendered in the docs.

value.description: A scalar quantity, or a list of identifiers for list-valued inputs such as a fitting list.

unit.description: Canonical unit of a quantity in the equation. SI-first. API callers may pass any convertible unit; this is the unit the spec and generated docs speak in, not the unit anything is calculated in - calculations work in SI base magnitudes, and to_si/from_si are the only places the two representations meet. Extend deliberately, with a conversion path in both languages: python/src/azoth/core/units.py's CANONICAL_UNITS, crates/azoth-core/src/units.rs's UNIT_NAMES, and a constructor in each. A contract test asserts the three lists are the same set, so adding a name to one and not the others fails rather than going unnoticed, and a conversion test asserts the round trip for every entry. SI-first is a convention for how these are written down, not a load-bearing property: mm is not its own SI base unit and converts correctly, because both implementations convert to base units rather than to the name recorded here.

type.description: quantity = a physical quantity carrying a unit. enum = a symbolic result such as a flow regime. fitting_list = one or more fitting ids resolved against the spec's `data.fittings` file.

values.description: Allowed values when type is enum.

optional.description: Optional inputs may be omitted; the implementation must then emit a RANGE_CHECK_SKIPPED warning for any range check that depends on them, rather than silently passing.

interval.description: The input is a temperature *difference* rather than an absolute temperature. Both are the same dimension, so a caller who passes 30 degC where a 30 K difference was meant gets 303.15 K: a plausible number wrong by 273.15, with nothing to catch it. Marking the input makes the Python boundary refuse an offset unit (degC, degF) rather than silently applying the offset - which is what Rust already gets for free by taking a TemperatureInterval rather than a ThermodynamicTemperature. Only meaningful on a unit that can express a difference, which is K; spec_lint enforces that.

quantity.description: Name of the quantity being bounded. Must be an input, an output, a derived quantity, or a state keyword such as `phase`.

computed_from.description: For derived quantities (e.g. Re), the inputs it is computed from. spec_lint uses this to prove the check is actually evaluable - a range check that cannot run is worse than none, because it looks like validation.

min.description: Lower bound of the interval described by min/max.

max.description: Upper bound of the interval described by min/max.

when.description: Which side of the min/max interval counts as a violation. 'outside' (the default) means the interval is the ALLOWED range, so values beyond it trigger the severity. 'inside' inverts this, for conditions that are only a problem within a band - e.g. transitional flow between Re 2000 and 4000. Only meaningful with min/max.

severity.description: error = mathematically undefined or invalid input, the implementation raises. warning = defined but outside the validated range, the implementation returns a value carrying a warning. Only evaluation of a test case may turn a `warning` range violation into a hard failure.

code.description: Which warning code a violation emits. Defaults to OUT_OF_VALID_RANGE, which is right for a plain bound. Override it when the violation has a more specific meaning - the transitional-flow band emits TRANSITIONAL_FLOW, so a caller can react to indeterminate friction without string-matching a message. The code is data, not behaviour: naming it here is what keeps the spec and the warning the code raises from drifting apart.

type.description: worked_example = the example above, re-generated into both languages. reference = an independent published or cross-method value. property = an invariant such as unit round-trip or symmetry.

status.description: skipped requires skip_reason. A skipped test is still generated, marked and reported - it is never silently dropped.

skip_reason.description: Why this test does not run, e.g. 'source_needed: citation could not be verified'.

property.description: Which invariant to check, when type is property.

source.description: Citation for the expected values, when type is reference.

allOf.comment: reference tests carry their own inputs and expected values, but only when they actually run - a skipped reference test has no expected values to state
property tests name the invariant they check
